summary: A satirical essay on how local development fragments wildlife habitat, using humor to describe subdivisions, malls and roads breaking up forests and meadows. It quotes an ecologist, a city planner and a professor, and mocks the claim that "animals will adapt." It closes by noting that fragmentation also mirrors the fragmentation of human communities.
one_line: A satirical essay mocking local development that fragments wildlife habitat and the glib assurance that animals will simply adapt.
key_facts: The essay is satire about habitat fragmentation and refers to the time before September 2023 as a period of uninterrupted meadows and forests.
Local ecologist Dr. Sylvia Green spoke out on September 5, 2023, saying critters prefer their homes 'like we prefer our pizzas: not in slices.'
Mr. Smith's new shopping mall has broken ground, fracturing former forests and reducing wildlife habitat to the size of postage stamps.
On October 10, 2023, city planner Bob "Bulldozer" Brown justified the latest subdivision, saying 'We'll throw in a couple of "wildlife crossings"—the critters will adapt!'
The resident badgers' burrows were replaced by a cul-de-sac and the badgers were not available for comment.
Dr. Green warns about edge effects, invasive species and loss of genetic diversity, which the essay jokes leaves deer in 'The Bachelor: Forest Edition.'
By the end of 2023, a study led by professor Ima Developer praised cookie-cutter homes next to former habitat of skunks, foxes and owls.
Professor Developer said that lawns the size of postage stamps mean 'a lot less mowing.'
The essay translates the mantra 'animals will adapt' as a demand that wildlife learn to cope with the built environment quickly or die, citing deer in headlights and roadkill risk from highways.
An expert named Kate argues that fragmented landscapes mirror fragmented human communities.
Billy the Raccoon, a fictional marketing guru, claims he lives in a storm drain but tells his kits it is waterfront property.
The essay ends by joking that a faint chirping could be either a bird or a construction truck back-up alarm.
